issues.legal_issue: A cohabiting relationship qualifies as a relationship in the nature of marriage only when its overall circumstances show essential characteristics of a marital relationship.
material_facts: The woman lived with the man for many years, knowing before the relationship began that he was married and had children.
The relationship was opposed by the man's wife and the woman's family.

There was no evidence that the couple presented themselves publicly as husband and wife, pooled resources, maintained joint financial arrangements, or gave each other mutual support and companionship.
The woman became pregnant three times, and each pregnancy was terminated; the court found no intention to rear children together.
issues.conclusion: The relationship was not in the nature of marriage and did not constitute a domestic relationship under the applicable definition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(f) and 2(s) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the court must assess the overall relationship and whether it has essential characteristics of marriage; the factors are illustrative and no single factor is conclusive. Relevant indicators include duration, a shared household, financial arrangements, domestic responsibilities, intimacy, children, public presentation as a couple, and the parties' intentions and conduct. The court relied on D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal for the distinction between a marriage-like relationship and mere cohabitation, and referred to Pinakin Mahipatray Rawal v. State of Gujarat on marital interests and obligations. It also considered the principles on presumptions from cohabitation in Andrahennedige Dinohamy, Badri Prasad, Tulsa, and Gokal Chand. A person who knowingly enters a relationship with someone already married cannot, on these facts, establish the exclusivity and monogamous character required for a relationship in the nature of marriage.

rule.if: protective_relief_claim and knowingly_partner_married and no_public_couple_presentation and no_joint_financial_life and no_children_intended and no_mutual_support_evidence

predicates.protective_relief_claim: A woman sought protective or financial relief on the basis of living with a man in a shared household.
predicates.knowingly_partner_married: The woman knew when the relationship began that the man was married to another person.
predicates.no_public_couple_presentation: The couple did not present themselves publicly or conduct themselves as spouses.
predicates.no_joint_financial_life: There was no evidence that the couple pooled resources or maintained joint financial arrangements.
predicates.no_children_intended: The circumstances showed that the couple did not intend to rear children together.
predicates.no_mutual_support_evidence: There was no evidence that the couple provided each other mutual support and companionship.

issues.definition: When a woman seeking relief based on cohabitation knew her partner was married and the relationship lacked public presentation as a couple, shared finances, an intention to rear children, and evidence of mutual support, the relationship is not treated as marriage-like.

issues.legal_issue: Ending a relationship that is not a domestic relationship covered by the Act and failing to maintain the former partner does not, without more, establish domestic violence under the Act.
material_facts: The woman sought relief under the Act after the man left the relationship and stopped maintaining her.
The courts below treated non-maintenance following the long relationship as domestic violence and ordered maintenance.

The Supreme Court found that the relationship was not in the nature of marriage and that there was no evidence of harm or abuse apart from the claimed failure to maintain her or continue the relationship.
issues.conclusion: The man's conduct in connection with this relationship did not amount to domestic violence under the Act, so the woman was not entitled to relief on that basis; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(a), 2(f), and 3 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 require an aggrieved person to have been in a covered domestic relationship and to allege conduct constituting domestic violence. Relief under Section 12, including the remedies described in Sections 18 to 22, depends on those requirements being met. The court applied its interpretation of a relationship in the nature of marriage under Section 2(f), and observed that the Act did not provide for the relationship at issue. It also referred to D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal in considering the character of the relationship.

predicates.domestic_violence_claim: A woman sought statutory relief alleging domestic violence arising from a cohabiting relationship.
predicates.relationship_outside_covered_domestic_ca: The relationship did not fall within the categories of domestic relationship covered by the law.
predicates.relationship_ended: The cohabiting relationship had ended when the woman sought relief.
predicates.no_proven_abusive_conduct_other_than_non: There was no proved abusive conduct apart from the former partner's failure to maintain the woman or continue the relationship.

issues.definition: If a domestic-violence claim arises from a relationship outside the covered categories, the relationship has ended, and the only proved conduct is non-maintenance, that conduct does not amount to domestic violence.
